speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not able-indeed, I am not sure that I would be physically able to do so-to lay on the Table a return asked for some long time ago, ordered by the House at the instance of the hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) calling for a list of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway. I have made inquiries, however, and I find that the return was asked for from the Grand Trunk through the President, Mr. Kelly, on October 23, 1919. He was asked to supply the names of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company as they appeared in the books of the company on October 19, 1919. I find that there has arrived a large packing case completely filled, containing the names of the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway; that it contains over 70,000 names and addresses; that it is available in the Records Branch of the Department of Railways and Canals and is there for the inspection of the hon. member for Cham-bly-Vereheres or any other member of the House or the Senate who desires to examine them. The memorandum furnished to me says that unfortunately it is not in duplicate but in handwritten form, on very large and specially ruled and printed sheets with nine separate columns covering each particular class of Grand Trunk stock. This list has been required in connection with the' Grand Trunk arbitration proceedings, and had to be sent twice to Montreal. It is in the Department at present and is available.

speechtext:
This is not an ad valorem duty, it is a duty based on the pound weight of the leaf tobacco. The duty is 40 cents a pound, fixed, of course, by the pound weight.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: The quality of the tobacco has nothing whatever to do with the duty?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: Has the minister not received representations or requests from cigar makers and others, especially the labouring class, in regard to this duty, inasmuch as it affects the price especially of cheap cigars? We do now see on the market as many cigars for five and ten cents as we used to see, and I understand that this is due to the fact that the duty
is based, not upon the value, but upon the weight. In the United States, I am informed, the duty is based upon the value and not upon the weight, so as to allow ordinary people to be able to get a better cigar at the same price. Some years ago I put similar questions to the Minister of Finance and he looked into the matter, and he was to investigate it more fully. Has any progress been made in this direction?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are two duties that are related to the matter to which my hon. friend refers. In the first instance, of course, we have our duty on the leaf tobacco, the raw material, and that duty, which is an excise duty is, as I have stated, 40 cents a pound. As my hon. friend intimates, many requests have been made for a change. Growers of tobacco-and we now grow a great deal of tobacco in Canada,- on the one hand have asked for a customs duty rate of $1 per pound on their product, and on the other hand manufacturers and the cigar makers, to whom my hon. friend has
4 p.m. referred, have made requests looking, not to an increase, but to a very substantial decrease in duties upon tobaccos manufactured in this country. The particular duty to which my hon. friend is referring is the excise duty on manufactured cigars. There is a great deal to be said on both sides, but it has been a subject which we felt, in view of other considerations, we could not at the present time interfere with. No change is made.

Mr. Chairman, this is really the most important item. I wonder if my hon. friend has made any comparative figures showing the relation of the raw sugar to the refined article. The sugar duties are very complicated, I know, varying at every degree of- the polaris-copic test, and it is very difficult for the ordinary reader to comprehend them, and one might easily make errors of calculation. I would be glad if my hon. friend could give the committee any comparative figures showing how far he is changing the duty on the raw material, and how far he is changing the duty as respects the refined article.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The matter is, as my hon. friend says, extremely complicated. We have to start with the preference which we are obliged to give the West Indies. Apply that minimum preference of 25 per cent, we start out with a base line, and having made that base line we make our Calculations; accordingly. There is a slight difference between the base line adopted for the British preferential tariff and that adopted for the general tariff. That had to be done in order to give effect to the preference called for
in the Act. The old base line for the British preferential was $1.52. That was the base line for the first of these items in No. 134. That is now being reduced to $1.50. Then for the purpose of carrying out the 25 per cent base line, the general tariff which was $1.93 becomes $2, and the matter works out progressively from that base line. The really important item, so far as the cost of sugar in this country is concerned, is the ninety-nine degree item, which gives us a rate of $1.79 for the British preferential tariff. The margin of protection on raw sugar which results, in the first instance, from item No. 134, and from item No. 135, does not in any way enlarge the protection on refining in Canada. This ninety-nine degree item, which is really the item of importance, resulting in a tax under the British preferential of $1.79, and $2.39 under the general tariff, may he compared to the tax in the United Kingdom for polarization, not under 98 degrees. The equivalent rate under the English law is $5.5763 as compared with our $2.39.

The matter is extremely complicated, I know. In the case of refined sugar you have to take 99 or 100

degrees, because it is of a high character, but if you take raw sugar at any figure, say, 90 degrees, perhaps the simplest way of explaining the matter would be for the minister to say what has been the duty heretofore on that, and what the new duty will be, and then we will see whether we are or are not having an increase on the raw material. If we make a similar computation with respect to the refined article, we can see how it works out. I am inclined to think, on first view- although I speak with reservation, -because I know how difficult it is to make exact calculations in these matters-that what my hon. friend has done is to reduce the rates of duty on raw material and increase the.duty on the refined article. It looks that way, but I do not wish to assert that too positively, because it would be necessary to make a careful computation before one could speak with absolute certainty. I thought my hon. friend would have some information on that point. Take sugar at 90 degrees; what does it pay now?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ninety-six degrees is the standard on which raw sugar is really purchased.
Much of it comes below that. A good deal of sugar is imported below 96.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The old item for raws under the British preferential tariff was $1.03J for 96 degrees as against 85.7 under the new order. The item which determines the question of protection is the general tariff item, which amounted to $1.37i, and the margin which is required by the agreement in connection with that, in schedule A of the treaty is 86.016 cents. The hon. gentleman will see that we have cut that down very materially in order to get that spread. If we did not cut it down on the British preferential side in order to get that spread there would have been a large increase in the customs duty. We expect to get no more revenue at all, but we hope to be able to hold the present revenue.

The raw material, practically speaking, will all come in under the West India Treaty, and we get our raw sugar very largely from the West Indies now. The aim of the West India agreement, very properly, is to increase purchases from the West Indies, and therefore I think it would be quite right to assume that the raw material will practically all come in under that agreement. If I understand my hon. friend on sugar of

96 degrees the rate hitherto charged was $1.03, and a fraction, and the new rate will be 85 cents. There is, therefore, a distinct reduction of 18 cents on the raw material. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is perfectly correct so far as the duty on the raw material is concerned. It has been cut down. We had to cut it down, or we should have had to increase the rate very much on the general standard. Although your preference is low, you do not buy at low prices. The exporter from the West Indies meets the competition which is open from the other fields, and I have been fortified in that conclusion by the remarks of my hon. friend in discussing the same question on previous occasions. Of course, human nature being what it is, my hon. friend was perfectly right; the benefit on all these preferences, generally speaking, will not come to the Canadian consumer; the benefit accrues to the exporter from the favoured country, unless, of course, the volume of trade is such that that advantage cannot be taken. But the fact is that the advantage can easily be taken. If I remember rightly, less than 50 per cent of our raw sugar manufactured in Canada comes from the British West Indies. I know I am quite right in saying that not more than 50 per cent comes from the West Indies, and it is perfectly obvious that there is not going to be any sugar bought in Canada at the lower standard having regard to that 50 per cent, and at the higher rate, having regard to the other 50 per cent.

The question as to
who gets the benefit is a rather complicated one, and it is not necessary, for our purpose, to discuss it. We must' confine ourselves to the duties; what their effect may be is a matter of argument. But if the legitimate aim on the West India agreement is to increase West India trade, it is a fair assumption that the bulk of our raw sugar-using that term broadly-will come from the West Indies. As a matter of fact, it comes largely from that section now, and under the agreement it will come in increasing qualities. Now, the rate on that raw sugar, which hitherto was $1.03, has been reduced to 85 cents, a distinct reduction-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
-a distinct reduction in favour of the refiner of 18 cents. There is no doubt about that. The only possible question is how much sugar may come from some other quarter and pay a

higher rate; but as the great aim of the West India agreement is for us to buy all the sugar we can from the West Indies, it is not unfair to assume that the bulk of our sugar will come from there, and to the extent that it does the refiner has an advantage of 18 cents, as compared with the previous rate. Having established the fact that the refiner is to get the raw material at a lower rate, let us turn to the question of the refined article.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You will have to establish that.

I think I have stated
the matter fairly.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is a
lower duty, but not a lower rate; it will not make the slightest difference in his rate.

We are not speaking
of anything but the duty now. I am taking my information from my hon. friend, and I speak with all deference, because I know . I could easily make a mistake in the matter. But I state the case again. Assuming that our raw sugar comes from the West Indies-and that is unquestionably the aim of the treaty, although, of course, occasionally, sugar will be imported from other places'-the rate hitherto paid having been $1,031 on sugar of 96 degrees, and the new rate being 85 cents, there is a distinct reduction to the refiner of 18 cents per hundred pounds.
Now if you turn to the refined article I think my hon. friend will find he is working the thing the, other way. When the West Indian Agreement was going through I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce if it did not imply a reduction on the raw material and he said it did. I then asked " What about the refined article?" He replied " That will have to be dealt with under the general tariff revision". Now, according to my figures I find thac while my hon. friend has reduced the duty on the raw material he has increased the duty on refined sugar, which is the only thing the people use. For all the purposes of refined sugar you have got to consider the operation of the preference-it will come from Great Britain, not from the United States. You are not going to get any considerable quantity of refined sugar from the United States. The most of that sugar that is coming in will come in under the British preference and, as I say, if my figures are correct, my hon. friend has reduced the duty on the raw material for the benefit of the refiner, and he has increased the duty on refined sugar which
is the only thing the people use. Now there is the possibility that an error has been made in the calculation and I would like to ask my hon. friend to check the figures.

Before the Minister of Finance answers my hon. friend, I would like to point out to him that a very large quantity of sugar, in fact nearly all that is used in the western sugar refinery, comes from Fiji.
Fiji is a British possession and is entitled to the preference.
It is not included in what my hon. friend referred to, the West Indian reciprocal agreement.

My hon. friend is
right. There would be a shade of difference in that respect, but he is quite correct.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No. I would like to have an answer from the Minister. He is reducing the duty to the refiner and I would like to know how the duty is increased on refined sugar.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was just
trying to follow a calculation and I did not quite catch what my hon. friend said.
There was nothing new in my last observation, it was merely a repetition.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend will find I am absolutely correct in this:	Competitive sugars in
the market, refined sugars, have always been foreign sugars. They have not been sugars manufactured in the West Indies, they have not been sugars manufactured under circumstances which can permit them to come in under the British preferential tariff. What we import under that tariff are raw sugars. The real competition in refined sugar-which as my hon. friend very properly says is the only thing that the people are interested in-is in foreign refined sugars chiefly from the United States where they get from time to time a very large quantity. Besides that there is a certain amount of refined sugar which comes in from the Orient; but the real competition, which affects the only market the Canadian consumer is directly interested in, is in refined sugar which comes from the United States. Taking refined sugar as of 99 and 100 degrees, as it is refined and sold, under the old tariff the rate per hundred pounds was 71 i cents. Under the present tariff the rate becomes

71 cents. In so far as the refiner in Canada is concerned his protection has been reduced by one-half of a cent having regard to his real competition. So far as regards the production of the raw materials for beet-root sugar on the other hand, the protection to the grower of beets has been largely increased. As the hon. gentleman says the public are interested in refined sugar, , ajid that is exactly the position.

The duties on refined sugar are so high that under ordinary conditions very little comes in. This last year or so we have had abnormal conditions, and it is not perhaps fair to judge by that, but a comparatively small part of refined sugar is imported into Canada. We produce our own refined sugar, and I am not desirous that it should be otherwise, but I think that my hon. friend will find that he has-whether he intended to do it or not-given the refiners some advantage they did not possess before. However, I do not want to delay the passing of the items at the present time. Before the matter is finally disposed of I will be very glad to check up the figures my hon. friend has given and see whether my own interpretation is different from his. I think we may take this item and the next one together because they are related one to the other.

Before we pass this item I would like to get an explanation from the minister of the proviso at the foot of item 134 which reads as follows:
Provided that refined sugar shall be entitled to entry under the British Preferential tariff upon evidence satisfactory to the Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue, that such refined sugar has been manufactured wholly from raw sugar produced in the British Colonies and possessions, and not otherwise.
Suppose that raw sugar produced in the island of Trinidad was imported into the United States and refined there. Can it come into Canada under the British preference?
'No.

This
language would seem to imply that it could, because it says that sugar that has been produced in the British colonial possessions, and refined is to have the benefit of the British preference. It is not declared that the sugar must come direct from the country of origin, apparently it may come from anywhere provided it is produced in a British colony. That is the

meaning of the language as I understand it. If I am incorrect in that understanding I would like to have an explanation from the minister.

I am afraid I am responsible for that language and I would like to explain the situation. Of course, nothing from the United States comes under the preferential tariff, whether it be sugar or anything else. The object of that clause is this: The aim under the former arrangement-and I am quite sure we are not desirous of changing it now- was to give a bona fide preference to the West Indies. If the West Indies can send their sugar to England and Scotland and have it refined there and come into Canada that sugar would bona fide be entitled to the preference, whereas if other sugars coming from foreign countries were sent to England and Scotland and refined there, if the British preference applied, it would not carry out the purpose of our agreement.

It
would be very easy to have a definition making it clear that the provision would apply to sugar coming from Great Britain or some of the British possessions:	The
present language is certainly open to the construction I have placed on it. Apparently the sugar may be refined anywhere provided the raw sugar was produced in a British colony. That seems to me to be the meaning of the sentence. If the intention is that it should apply where sugar produced in a British colony like Trinidad or Jamaica, and was afterwards refined in Great Britain or in any British possession, and subsequently introduced into Canada, it would be quite easy to claim language that would cover such a case.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think anything has worked out wrongly or that there has been any real difficulty under the wording of this clause. It is a clause which was, I think, the subject of a great deal of careful study by my hon. friend the ex-Finance Minister in introducing what is really, after all, the whole bases of this particular kind of trade convention -his British preferential tariff of 1897. The wording of that Act stands unchanged, and we are merely continuing what in the light of experience has been found to work well.

I admit that the
clause standing alone would be capable of that interpretation, but as the British

preference is distinctly confined to British countries, I think it is quite evident you have to read that into the clause.
For years it has worked out all right under this interpretation.

The resolution says distinctly that articles specified in schedule A. shall not be subject at any time to more than fifty per cent of the duties imposed on similar goods as set forth in the general tariff. This means that a number of these items scheduled in the general tariff would be allowed to come into Canada at a very much lower rate of duty than the same articles coming from Great Britain.
I am sure that cannot be the intention of the Government.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know anything in that section in which Great Britain is interested in the slightest. She does not grow sugar, limes or shaddocks. This is done having regard particularly to West Indian products, and the Act is entirely followed in the present resolution.
Does not Great Britain manufacture sugar?
Not raw sugar.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Sugar is
exempt from that provision.

What about fruits, items
103	and 104?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is no preference given to those items; those are fruits preserved in brandy.

The resolution states, of course, the exception, "goods, other than tobacco, cigars, cigarettes, spirituous, or alcoholic liquors;" but these items 103 and
104	refer distinctly to preserved fruits. We get a quantity of preserved fruits from England and Scotland. Unless you dot every "i" and cross every "t" in the resolution, the department is likely to put a strictly literal interpretation on the Act, as, for instance, what happened last year in their classification of manufacturers, resulting in an immense amount of trouble. I would like to see this Bill put in such form that when it is passed no room will be left open for any expensive law suits -expensive on the Government and on individuals-caused by (too literal rulings of the department.

If Great Britain produces the same articles, undoubtedly the argument of my hon. friend is correct and
me rates of duty would vary. The only answer of the minister is that Great Britain does not produce the same things as a rule. It may be so in regard to fruit. It is a well understood principle that in no case will we charge Great Britain a higher duty than any other country. But as this resolution is worded there is nothing to say we shall not charge goods from Great Britain a higher rate than similar goods from the West Indies, and I am afraid we are going to do it under this agreement if there is any competition.

It was expressly provided in the agreement with the West Indies that we should be at perfect freedom to make arrangements, preferential and otherwise, and that the West Indies should have the same liberty. The West Indies gives us a quid pro quo for which it gets a concession from us. Great Britain does not give us that quid pro quo, so we have a perfect right under the agreement with the West Indies to charge the lesser rate of duty agreed upon, and to charge on articles coming from the other parts of the Empire a preferential rate.
My right hon. friend is getting back to the very old ground that we should not give England a preference unless she gives us a quid pro quo.
But we do.
We do without a quid pro quo. My right hon. friend says we are justified in not giving it to England because she does not give us a quid pro quo.

England has .a preferential tariff of thirty per cent now, although she does not give us a quid pro quo. We do not take that preference away from her; but when we make an agreement with the West'Indies under which they give us reciprocity, and we give it to them in return, I do not think there is any injustice done to England.

If you will permit me to refer back to the items that have already been passed to clear up the situation, items Nos. 20, 21, 22 and 23, I think it will be admitted that if these schedules are to obtain as they stand there will be a distinct discrimination against Great Britain in respect to those items. They are cocoa, paste or "liquor," preparations of cocoa or chocolate in powder form, preparations of cocoa or chocolate not otherwise provided for and confectionery. According to my reading of the resolution, those will be imported from

the Wejt Indies at a very much lower rate of duty than from Great Britain under this Act as. it reads. Therefore we are discriminating against Great Britain.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I appreciate the point my hon. friend makes. The fact is that none of those items he has referred to are produced in the West Indies; they have none of those manufactures there. They are very much interested in the cocoa bean, Item 77A, and, indeed, that is the item which necessitates the changes that my hon. friend has referred to. The West Indies produce the cocoa bean, and England manufactures it into these commodities, as my hon. friend says. We also manufacture it into the same commodities. The West Indies are only interested in getting their preference in connection with the cocoa bean, which is given to them as called for by the agreement.

Any regulation which guards against fraud should have our sympathy. It is a question, however, as to how far it is wise to do this thing by law. There is something in a reputation which is established by the makers of a certain article, and the stamp on Scotch woollen goods is of as much value as if legally enacted. I am afraid this law will lead to some trouble. I notice in the next clause that provision is made for this section to come into force on September last. That would penalize people for goods they already have in their possession.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The next section provides for this regulation becoming effective on September 1, 1921.

I beg my hon. friend's pardon. Of course, if similar Acts are in force elsewhere we may be able to learn something from them. Would there not be difficulty in marking large bales of these goods? And when you say they are to be marked so as to indicate the country of origin, would goods from the Old Country have to be marked as coming from England, Scotland, Ireland or the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should say
the United Kingdom.

Then you may have
some cheap English goods masquerading as Scotch goods.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Or still worse, Irish goods.

And you would be
doing some injustice to Old Ireland.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is right.

I think there is a ,
little vagueness in this section which may be embarrassing. I know the difficulty of going into details in regard to these things, but it is so hard to know where the mark can be placed on some articles. Take a man who has a roll of cloth in his shop, and he sells off twenty yards of it; the roll was marked on the edge; after selling twenty yards what evidence have you got on the remainder as to where it came from? The penalties are severe, and while the object is a good one, I rather think the hon. gentleman will find difficulty in enforcing the regulation.

I think Old Country firms are manufacturing goods now to be imported here this autumn, and therefore three months is not enough notice to all the world that all goods imported to Canada after September 1, 1921, have to be marked. I would say that six months' notice at least ought to be given.

I should say you do not run any risk if you leave the date as it is, because any firm which is proud of its goods will take care to mark them so the public will know what they are buying. It is only those who are not proud of their goods who will not be anxious to mark them.

I agree with the member for Shelburne and Queen's that in matters of this kind

indeed, in all matters- the public have a right to be protected. But the enforcement of a law of this class is absolutely impossible, having regard to the strict wording of the provision of it. During the last year we have had some difficulty in connection with the interpretation of an Act. We were assured by the minister in charge of the Bill when the legislation was before the House that it would be subject to a certain interpretation but when the customs officers came to enforce it they interpreted its provisions quite differently. The result was no end of trouble during the last year, including a law-suit

which has just been concluded, and which will be very expensive to whoever has to pay the costs.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid that we have to pay them.

But only a certain proportion. I am not a lawyer, but I understand that only certain costs can he assessed by a solicitor against the loser of a case; the other party will always have something to pay. Now, this provision insists on the branding of goods which may be branded without injury. Who is to decide what articles may be branded without injury? Some customs official who knows nothing about the material he is handling? Then there is a penalty provided of $1,000 and a year's imprisonment. It is provided also that all goods imported into Canada which do not comply with the requirements made shall be subject to an additional duty of 10 per cent and shall not be released from the customs office until they have been branded. Who is to do the branding? Some official in the Customs Department who knows nothing about the goods he is handling? Mr. Chairman, I would like to see this resolution struck out. If it is adopted we shall have a serious condition to deal with-a more serious condition than prevailed in connection with the Luxury Tax Act and the definition of what is a manufacturer. Now, you ask your customs officials to go into a retail store to examine a line of goods-officials who know very little of the technical qualities of the goods they are inspecting. And who is going to say whether or not the goods should be branded? It is provided that they shall be marked in a conspicuous place. Take the case of stockings; what lady is going to wear a pair of stockings which are branded with an indelible stamp?
Skirts may get longer.

Unfortunately, Mr. Chairman, they do not show a tendency in that direction. It is the other way about, so it is hard to say what may happen in that regard. Prior to the war a law was passed in England providing that goods which were not made in Great Britain should be marked "not British manufacture." That created a good deal of hard feeling in Germany. But the British manufacturers decided that in handling goods marked "German manufacture," for instance, they were advertising German manufactures; accordingly, they came to the conclusion that they would avoid that result by having the goods marked 'not British manufacture." If it were provided that the packages or containers of the goods should be marked "British manufacture," "German manufacture" or "Swiss /manufacture," as the case might be, the purpose my hon. friend has in mind would be served, but such a law as is proposed cannot be enforced without a great deal of trouble and a considerable amount of friction. Some one has said that a good deal of deception is practiced by retail merchants by selling goods as of Scotch, English or Irish manufacture which are not made in those countries. Well, I suggest that the public should be allowed to do some deciding on their own account; they should be educated to the point of toeing able to protect themselves against impositions of that kind. I have seen any amount of tweed goods which had been made in Canada sold as Scotch manufacture. It suits the purchaser's fancy to believe that he is buying goods of Scotch manufacture, and he ig getting value for his money just the same. A certain amount of that sort of thing cannot possibly be avoided,-and when clothing made in Canada is sold as Scotch goods, I do not think the purchaser suffers very much as a result. Of course, I want it to be understood distinctly that I do not approve of deception of that kind. Some of the best carpets produced are made in Canada. I would not have to go far from this chamber to find goods in use marked "British manufacture" and "U.S. manufacture" which, if the purchaser knew his business, would be found to be not so good value for the money as goods manufactured in Canadian mills.
Another point is this: .If you insist on this resolution being put into force, you increase the cost of commodities, because all these little additional operations cost money. I do not think we should endeavour to stop the present downward trend of the price of commodities, and every little hampering enactment of this kind will certainly add to the cost of merchandise because it will cost money to brand each individual item in a package. If you brand the package or container, that will be quite sufficient to indicate where the goods come from, and the purpose underlying this resolution will be served by an enactment along this line. I shall be sorry if the minister insists on passing this resolution, because I know he will find that it will cause a great deal of hardship and trouble, particularly as regards merchandise in stock on September 1. 1921.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not interfered with.

Your customs officer, inspector, or spotter who goes around the country will interfere. He has been interfering in other cases. He will go into a store and find one line of articles that have been imported after September 1 and that are branded, and another line of the same goods not branded. What will he do? He will purchase an article that is not branded, take it before a magistrate and lay an information, and the merchant will have to defend a case of that kind. The minister need not shake his head. I have been through the mill, and I know exactly what this means. The retail trade of this country will >be put to a great deal of cost in defending cases of this kind. Officials who have very little knowledge of items in which they are dealing, will put not only the department, but the business of the country to a great deal of trouble that might be saved by leaving conditions as they are.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I assure my hon. friend at once that this is something where there is no room for misunderstanding. Last year we did not get the legislation quite as clear as we should have done. I thought it was clear and evidently the courts thought it was clear enough, but the decision was overruled. There is no question of courts here. This is a question of the administration of the customs office pure and simple. You do not send inspectors out of the customs office unless they are asked to go and look after something special. There would certainly be no scrutiny made of private stocks after September 1, for the purpose of finding what had not been marked. The whole idea of this law is that when customs entries are being made and goods are being examined for customs purposes, then and then only shall this question as to the marking be determined. One might just as well say that because you have a customs law as it is now, the customs officer must follow everybody into the different offices, warehouses and so forth for the purpose of worrying and annoying him. As regards trade matters, I have very often the pleasure of agreeing with my hon. friend, but I think he is mistaken as regards a system which allows a Canadian manufacturer, in the case that he quoted, to turn around and sell Canadian-made goods, no matter how good they may be, as 
Scotch goods. I do .it ; think that is a proper system.

I do not think it is a
good system.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are going a long way in stopping that sort of thing by this legislation. Moreover, during the war, the people of this country were badly taken in in matters of this kind. First-rate hats are made in Canada; but during the war, hats were sold as English hats, and the only things that were English on them were the label and the hat band. If we get everything marked properly when it comes in, the proper mark of the firm, the mark can be put on any way they like. They are not going to hurt the smallest things. I yield at once to my hon. friend's experience in ladies' stockings, but I have seen very good ladies' stockings with marks on the toes. I have even seen those sacred things injured to the extent of having the number on them, and I do not believe it would hurt them any more if we put the name of the country on the toe. I do not believe that ladies would object to that in the slightest. As regards what kind of goods should be marked, that is something that will have to be made final, definite and determined in the regulations. There are some goods that ought not to be marked.
Mr. PEDIjOW: j The resolution says that the article must be marked in a conspicuous place and thdt the mark must not be covered up.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that a lady's stocking is, of necessity, conspicuous in the sense that he means? I think my hon. friend is having a little fun at my expense, and that he really understands the object of the resolution; that is, that when a purchase is made by the consumer, the consumer will be able to see somewhere on the article, in a place where it can be read, the name of the country of origin. I do not think my hon. friend would say that, if that were applied to corsets, the name could not be put on a conspicuous place on the corsets. It refers to the garment, not when worn, but when purchased.

Might I suggest to the
minister that during the recess he might gather for the committee such information as would enable us to determine to what extent this prevails in other countries, because this will largely affect international trade? If it is a good

thing for Canada to introduce and enforce such regulations, other countries may determine that it is a good thing for their trade, and this might result in a considerable expense to those throughout our country who do an export business.

Would it not be a
move further in the right direction to require that goods manufactured in Canada shall be stamped as being of Canadian manufacture, so that we might stop the fraud of which my hon. friend speaks, of Canadian goods being sold as British goods? If it is good policy to let the people of Canada know that these goods are made abroad, it is equally good policy to let them know the goods that are made at home.
I foresee another difficulty. We have by regulations and the customs tariff dealt with the British preference, that is to say in determining what the country of origin is. For example, German goods are advanced to a stage nearing perfection. They are then sent to Great Britain where they are finished. When they come over here, is Great Britain the country of their origin? In the case of the British perference, there must be a certain percentage of British labour on them to enable them to be recognized as coming under our tariff. I am afraid my hon. friend will meet that same difficulty in determining the country of origin.
At Six o'clock, the committee rose and the House took recess.

On the Orders of the Day:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I feel impelled again to refer to a matter that was introduced into this House by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), in the course of his speech in the Budget debate on Thursday last. In that speech he made a statement in reference to a subject which I freely say he should not have felt at liberty to discuss in the House. He said that an offer had been made by me, or by some one representing me, of a position in this Government to Hon. Mr. Veniot, the Minister of Public Works in the province of New Brunswick. At the time I gave a categorical denial to the assertion, and added that no one, on my authority, had made any such proposal. The subject was brought up again, at yesterday's sitting of the House, some time this morning by the member for Russell (Mr. Murphy.)
Centre Vancouver.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It was brought up by the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), in relation to certain changes which he stated had been made in the report in Hansard.
It was referred to by the hon. member for Russell, however, proceeding along the line of the hon. member for Marquette, and an interview, or an alleged interview, said to have been given by the hon. Mr. Veniot, in his own province, was read. In the interview it was alleged-I am not saying now that the allegation was made by the hon. member for Russell; I do not know of my own knowledge whether the interview was ever given or not that this gentleman had been approached on behalf of myself, and indeed went on to say that some letter had been written to him by me and-
No, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is the way it appeared in Hansard transcript, although I see in the paper-
Hansard was corrected.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-Mr. Veniot said it had been written to somebody else by me. This was intended to confirm the allegation that this proposal had been made. During all this I knew from memory, although

my correspondence is very heavy, that I had received some letter some time on the subject, hut as no one was good enough to give me the name of the correspondent I was not able to trace it. My secretary tried to do so yesterday but without success. This forenoon he has succeeded in securing two letters written me by a gentleman in the city of St. John. I am sorry to have to give so much time and attention to this subject. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the House, it is not worth it, but those responsible are well known.
I am sorry also that letters of this character that were not intended by the writer to be made public are under the necessity of being made public because of the very unusual-and I hope not to be repeated- action taken by certain hon. members. I therefore propose to lay on the Table the actual correspondence that passed between us, and I commend it to the consideration of the hon. members who have not only been the means of circulating through this country an impression wholly false-I had almost said cruelly false-but an impression that has been taken advantage of by one or two unprincipled newspapers to pursue tactics peculiar to themselves. The first letter is dated November 29-1 am not sure that I personally read it wholly through when I got it. I may say before I proceed any further that what I hold in my hand is all the correspondence that passed between me and anybody on the subject; nor did I speak to any human being, Cabinet minister, or other, on the subject. All I had to do with it is as represented by the correspondence I now read:
Saint John, N.B., November 29, 1920. Honourable Arthur Meighbn,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Premier,-
I have just read the article "Trying to Rope Him In'' by "The Mace" in this week's Toronto Saturday Night, and naturally it makes one think of "How to do it".
Not having had the pleasure of meeting you I am an entire stranger, but we have some" mutual friends and to one, W. F. O'Connor, Ottawa, I will refer you as to my good faith in any proposition I may make.
Everybody knows how big the job is "To rope him in" and nearly all look at it from the same view point. My idea is to get at it from a different angle. Let me explain briefly: At the time of forming Union Government, I wrote Sir Robert L. Borden and suggested that, as he could not get support in Quebec, it would be good policy to take in the Honourable Peter J. Veniot who had two or three sons overseas, who could easily be returned for Gloucester, N.B., and who is well and favourably known throughout Eastern Quebec, but Sir Robert did not act on the suggestion although he wrote me In favour of it.
I may say that he was not in favour of it. I have the letter that was written.
You want and must get French support and Cabinet material. Why not take Mr. Veniot as representative of the Acadians among whom all over the Maritime Provinces he is recognised as leader. He would quickly increase his following from Quebec where he is active in many French organizations etc., and if desired at general election he could easily stand for and carry a Quebec riding. It would strengthen you with the French speaking people and be a powerful factor in breaking the solid front against you and the means of changing opponents to supporters.
In the words of the article referred to "You need a Tarte". Well Mr. Veniot is next thing to a Tarte, a trained parliamentarian, good debater, fluent speaker in both English and French, clever political organizer, stands well with his Church authorities and both French and English speaking people, knows the political game and so far has made good as Minister of Public Works for New Brunswick.
If you looked upon the suggestion with favour the question would be "Could you get him?" I have not spoken to Mr. Veniot about it nor to any other person in his behalf and he has not the faintest idea that I am writing you or had written Sir Robert Borden.
One way to win is to think of schemes others overlook and act upon them and this is such a case and I believe it can be put through.
Of course Mr. Veniot would have a portfolio in Cabinet. To make an opening for him Mr. Turgeon would have to be provided for and Mr. Veniot for the time being, at least, represent Gloucester. Probably Mr. Veniot would look upon the change to get to Ottawa with favour in view of the Farmers gain made in the last Provincial election in the English districts looked after by other ministers. He put the Foster Government into power and if he withdrew it ^ would quickly go out which would mean a coalition between Conservatives and Farmers with Baxter for Premier and such would be a great factor towards your success later.	!
Almost the entire gain in population in the Maritime Provinces is among the Acadians. There are two Acadian Bishops in New Brunswick and giving Acadians recognition in Federal Cabinet would be simple justice in ^ proportion to populations, and create favorable impressions all over the Maritime provinces.
If I could be of any service in this matter let me know. I thought possibly if we found Mr. Veniot favourable it might be arranged for him to board your train at some quiet station and discuss the matter with you en route to or from Sydney, C.B., as I see you are going there.
Yours truly,
The signature is here. I would like hon. members to state further whether they desire to have it; if necessary we can discuss that. I do not know the gentleman; I never heard of him.
It does not make any difference.	'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. members of finer feeling will see that it might be better that his name should not he given. I am sorry to have had to read the letter. Now I will read my reply.
You might give his initials.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
If I am asked by the leader of the Opposition to give the name I will give it. My reply is dated December 1, and is very brief.
Ottawa, Ont., Deoember 1, 1920.
I have just received your letter of the 29th November. I will discuss the subject to which you call attention with Mr. Wig-more. I have had no intimation whatever from the party to whom you refer as <to his attitude towards the Government or toward the paramount Federal issues of the day.
Faithfully yours,
(Sgd.) Arthur Meighen.
I received, I see, a further letter dated January 7, from the same gentleman which reads as follows:
St. John, N.B., January 7, 1921. Honourable Arthur Meighen,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Meighen :-
After receipt of your letter and a letter from Mr. Wigmore, I awaited Mr. Wigmore's visit which was delayed and unfortunately missed seeing him, although I endeavoured to do so.
As you and Mr. Wigmore may not be in Ottawa at the same time I enclose oopy of the letter I am sending Mr. Wigmore which explains itself.
The interviews referred to therein did not lessen my faith in the suggestion but rather confirmed it.
If I can be of any service in this or any other matter to assist you kindly advise.
Yours truly,
To which I replied as follows on January 10:
Ottawa, Ont., January 10, 1921.
On my return to the city I find your letter of the 7th January, together with copy of one addressed to Mr. Wigmore, Minister of Customs, with whom I will be glad to discuss the matter referred to, at the first favourable opportunity.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) Arthur Meighen.
I may say that through pressure of work or otherwise I have never yet even spoken to the Minister of Customs on the subject.
I should read now the letter to the Minister of Customs, a copy of which was enclosed to me in the above letter of January 7.
It is dated January 7, 1921, and is as follows:
Dear Mr. Wigmore
I am sorry you were unable to see me during your visit to Saint John as per your letter of December 3. I called at your office four or five times each day and the third day left a letter offering to meet you at any time or place that would suit you best, and repeatedly phoned and left my number both at the office and Mr. Terry's.

I know how rushed you were and merely mention above to show I did my best to see you without breaking my other business engagements.
I was in Bathurst two weeks since I got your letter and had three interviews with the party about whom I had written the Premier, and while I was not in a position to say anything definite, I promised to see him after your visit and now not having seen you puts me in an awkward position.
I might say in a general way my friend is quite an admirer of the Premier whom he met once in Ottawa, and believes in his sincerity to give the Dominion good honest administration and admits need of tariff and other methods of taxation to raise revenue to carry on affairs of this great country. He did not turn the proposition down, felt details as I suggested to make opening, could easily be arranged, but until I had something more definite he did not wish to say more than that he would be glad to see me after my interview with you.
As, expecting to see you, I delayed acknowledging the Premier's letter. I am doing so to-day and enclosing him carbon o-f this letter so he will know how the matter stands if you and he do not be in Ottawa at the same time.
.	Yours truly,
I have already read the letter in which he enclosed this copy.
You have not read the letter of Mr. Wigmore to this gentleman.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, I want to keep distinct the correspondence with myself; then I will read that letter.
This is the entire correspondence with me. There has been nothing beyond the correspondence, not a word-not even a sight of the gentleman, not even a word to my colleague or to any other members of the Government.
Did I understand the right hon. gentleman to say that the man's name was signed to this letter?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Is it signed on the copy?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I will lay it on the Table with the signature to it when asked by the leader of the Opposition.
I am simply asking if this copy is signed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the signature was copied on the typewriter, but the original letter was signed. On receipt of the letters, in the usual way I had my secretary refer them to the appropriate minister, and he put on the face of the correspondence:
Hon. R. W. Wigmore.
Referred by the Prime Minister for consideration.
George F. Buskard,
Private Secretary.

Mr. Wigniore then writes:
The Prima Minister has referred to me your letter in reference to P. J. Veniot and X have carefully noted what you say. I expect to he in St. John between Christmas and New Tears and will be very glad to discuss the matter personally with you then.
Which discussion did not take place.

When yesterday the Prime Minister denied these letters he quoted the speech of the member for Russell in this way:
The person who made the overtures to me presented to me a letter addressed to me and signed Premier Meighen.
I find the quotation in the unrevised Hansard reads:
The person who made the overtures to me presented to me a letter addressed to him and signed by Premier Meighen.
The Prime Minister when reading the quotation said: "addressed to me." That was not quite what the hon. member for Russell had quoted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
will recall that the hon. member for Russell declined to read the interview in my hearing when I came into the House. I therefore sent to the Hansard office for the transcript; I received it, and it read exactly as I read in the House. I have the transcript in my hand at this moment. I presume there is an error.

It does not read that way
in the unrevised Hansard this morning.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I hold in my hand the transcript handed to me by the Hansard office. That possibly may be clear as well. Let me say finally, that what I stated was this, that no such proposal had been made by me, or upon my authority, directly or indirectly, definitely or indefinitely, or in any other way. I appeal to my colleagues of this House whether what I said was right.

I notice in reading the
Journal newspaper report that there was mention of a letter sent by the Prime Minister to Mr. Veniot on January 11. Is there such a letter in the hands of the Prime Minister?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There was no such
letter received. I never wrote him, and he never wrote me-at least, none was received.
